title: Antitrust on Aisle Five: How Well Do Divestiture Remedies Work?
summary: This paper examines the long-run effectiveness of structural divestiture remedies used by antitrust authorities in merger cases. Using census-level establishment data and proprietary transaction records from the U.S. grocery sector, the authors find that divested stores experience an average 31 percent decline in employment over five years, driven by elevated exit rates and persistent contraction. The authors conclude that structural remedies may be less effective when merging parties retain substantial discretion over which assets are divested and to which buyers.
key_points: Divested stores experience an average 31 percent decline in employment over five years post-remedy
Employment decline is driven by elevated store exit rates and persistent contraction among surviving establishments
Sales also decline following divestiture, indicating sustained operational impact
Transaction-level evidence shows divested assets are systematically weaker (lower capability) than comparable non-divested stores
Assets are often transferred to lower-capability buyers, potentially undermining remedy effectiveness
The paper suggests structural remedies may be less effective when implementation allows merging parties discretion over asset selection and buyer choice
why_it_matters: This research provides empirical evidence on whether antitrust divestiture remedies achieve their intended goal of maintaining competition. For policymakers and regulators reviewing merger proposals, the findings suggest that implementation details—specifically how much discretion parties have over assets and buyers—may critically determine whether a structural remedy preserves competitive outcomes or merely transfers assets to weaker operators.
